steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Transformer-based Language Model (LM) performance depends a lot on three scaling factors, which are the number of model parameters, the size of the pretraining dataset, and the amount of computing. To get the best performance all three of these factors have to be scaled up at the same time. This scaling law has brought several challenges for research in neural language modeling. One big obstacle is that resources are not distributed equally across languages. Because of this, the current approach of transformer-based models does not reach equally high performance levels for models made for different languages.

There is also a big difference between the way LMs learn and the way humans acquire language. One difference is about the data that is the input to learning. LMs like BERT, RoBERTa or GPT-3 see billions of tokens during training, which is far more than what an individual human sees when learning a language. This basic discrepancy raises important considerations when we draw parallels between language learning in machines and in humans.

One direction for making LMs more data-efficient is to change the model architecture. An approach that works well here is to put an inductive bias into the architecture of the models, which could possibly help the model acquire more knowledge from the same amount of data than standard models do. But what type of inductive bias should be added is still being explored. Recently there have been efforts looking at syntactic hierarchical inductive biases as a possible improvement.

One of these possible solutions is the StructFormer architecture. It is a transformer that is trained on the masked language modeling task. There is an additional convolutional neural network (CNN) component which produces unlabeled dependency and constituency trees as a byproduct, and it influences the self-attention mechanism of the transformer layers. The model got competitive results in structure induction evaluations and it decreased perplexity compared to a vanilla transformer baseline. However it is still an open question if the inductive bias learned in this architecture makes performance better on downstream NLP tasks.

- Our work
  - pretrain StructFormer on data from a different domain, not tested on it before
  - more sophisticated tokenizer vs. most-frequent-words dictionary from original experiment
  - modify architecture: hierarchical bias in the middle layers instead of after the embedding layer -> better downstream?
  - evaluate seven model variants with shared task evaluation pipeline, submit best one

## The BabyLM Challenge
- shared task, data-efficient language modeling for English; pretrain LM from scratch on about as much data as a child gets
- good setting: pretraining dataset, thorough evaluation pipeline, comparison with other participating systems
- two tracks: 100M words corpus, 10M words sample of it
- size from children hearing 2M-7M words per year (cite); mostly spoken -> lots of transcribed data from different domains (domains: cite)
- 39 evaluation tasks: efficiency and applied NLP, cognitive science, linguistics
- BLiMP 17 tasks zero-shot; SuperGLUE and MSGS need finetuning for classification; full list in Appendix A

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Transformer-based Language Model (LM) performance depends a lot on three scaling factors, which are the number of model parameters, the size of the pretraining dataset, and the amount of computing. To get the best performance all three of these factors have to be scaled up at the same time. This scaling law has brought several challenges for research in neural language modeling. One big obstacle is that resources are not distributed equally across languages. Because of this, the current approach of transformer-based models does not reach equally high performance levels for models made for different languages.

There is also a big difference between the way LMs learn and the way humans acquire language. One difference is about the data that is the input to learning. LMs like BERT, RoBERTa or GPT-3 see billions of tokens during training, which is far more than what an individual human sees when learning a language. This basic discrepancy raises important considerations when we draw parallels between language learning in machines and in humans.

One direction for making LMs more data-efficient is to change the model architecture. An approach that works well here is to put an inductive bias into the architecture of the models, which could possibly help the model acquire more knowledge from the same amount of data than standard models do. But what type of inductive bias should be added is still being explored. Recently there have been efforts looking at syntactic hierarchical inductive biases as a possible improvement.

One of these possible solutions is the StructFormer architecture. It is a transformer that is trained on the masked language modeling task. There is an additional convolutional neural network (CNN) component which produces unlabeled dependency and constituency trees as a byproduct, and it influences the self-attention mechanism of the transformer layers. The model got competitive results in structure induction evaluations and it decreased perplexity compared to a vanilla transformer baseline. However it is still an open question if the inductive bias learned in this architecture makes performance better on downstream NLP tasks.

In this paper we pretrain the StructFormer architecture on a dataset from a different domain, which had not been tested on that model before. We also use a more sophisticated tokenizer, compared to the most frequent words dictionary that was used to train the models in the original experiment. We also modify the model architecture to see if injecting a hierarchical bias in the middle layers of the transformer architecture (and not after the embedding layer) leads to better downstream performance. In the end we evaluate seven model variants with the evaluation pipeline of the shared task and we submit our best model to the shared task challenge.

## The BabyLM Challenge

The BabyLM Challenge is a shared task whose aim is data-efficient language modeling for English. The participants pretrain a LM from scratch on data that corresponds to the amount of linguistic data that a child has available. This task is a great setting for our experiments. It gives us a pretraining dataset and a thorough evaluation pipeline, and it also gives us an environment where we can compare the performance of our models to other interesting architectures from the systems that participate in the shared task.

The shared task has two tracks with different dataset sizes, a 100M words corpus and a 10M words corpus which is a sample of the larger corpus. The size comes from the assumption that children are exposed to 2M-7M words per year. Since children mostly interact with spoken language data and not written language data, the datasets include a high proportion of transcribed data from different domains. More details about the source domains can be found in another source.

Every model participating in the shared task is evaluated with a thorough evaluation pipeline with 39 different tasks. These tasks are supposed to represent the performance of a model with respect to efficiency and applied NLP, and also cognitive science and linguistics. A group of 17 tasks, called BLiMP, are done with zero-shot predictions, while the other two groups of tasks, SuperGLUE and MSGS, need finetuning of the submitted models for classification. The complete list of tasks is in Appendix A.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Transformer-based Language Model (LM) performance is heavily influenced by three scaling factors: the number of model parameters, the pretraining dataset size, and the amount of computing. For optimal performance, all three factors have to be scaled up simultaneously [1]. This scaling law has introduced several challenges in advancing research on neural language modeling. One major obstacle is the unequal distribution of resources across languages. As a result, the current approach of transformer-based models falls short of achieving equally high performance levels for models dedicated to different languages [2].

Moreover, there is a considerable difference between the way LMs learn and the way humans acquire language. One difference concerns the data that is input to learning: LMs such as BERT [3], RoBERTa [4] or GPT-3 [5] are exposed to billions of tokens during training, far more than what an individual human is exposed to when learning a language [6]. This fundamental discrepancy raises important considerations when drawing parallels between language learning in machines and humans.

One direction for improving the data-efficiency of LMs is to adapt the model architecture. An effective approach here is to incorporate an inductive bias into the models' architectures, which could potentially help them acquire more knowledge from the same amount of data than standard models. However, the specific type of inductive bias to add is still under exploration. Recently, there have been efforts to investigate syntactic hierarchical inductive biases as a potential improvement [7,8].

One of these potential solutions is the StructFormer architecture [9], a transformer trained on the masked language modeling task. An additional convolutional neural network (CNN) component produces unlabeled dependency and constituency trees as a byproduct and influences the self-attention mechanism of the transformer layers. The model has shown competitive results in structure induction evaluations and a decrease in perplexity over a vanilla transformer baseline [10]. However, it remains an open question whether the inductive bias learned in this architecture improves performance on downstream NLP tasks.

We pretrain the StructFormer architecture on a dataset from a different domain that had not been tested on that model before. We also use a more sophisticated tokenizer than the most frequent words dictionary used to train the models in the original experiment. Additionally, we modify the model architecture to investigate whether injecting a hierarchical bias in the middle layers of the transformer architecture (rather than after the embedding layer) leads to better downstream performance. Finally, we evaluate seven model variants through the evaluation pipeline of the shared task and submit our best-performing model to the shared task challenge.

## 1.1 The BabyLM Challenge

The BabyLM Challenge is a shared task aimed at data-efficient language modeling for English. Participants pretrain a LM from scratch on data corresponding to the amount of linguistic data available to a child. The task is a great setting for our experiments. It provides a pretraining dataset, a thorough evaluation pipeline, and also an environment where we can compare our models' performance to other interesting architectures from the systems participating in the shared task.

The shared task has two tracks with different dataset sizes: a 100M words corpus, and a 10M words corpus sampled from the larger corpus. The size is inspired by the assumption that children are exposed to 2M-7M words per year [11]. Since children mostly interact with spoken rather than written language data, the datasets include a high proportion of transcribed data from different domains. For more details on the source domains, please refer to [12].

Every model participating in the shared task is evaluated with a thorough evaluation pipeline comprising 39 different tasks. These tasks are meant to represent a model's performance with respect to efficiency and applied NLP, as well as cognitive science and linguistics. A group of 17 tasks, named BLiMP [13], is performed via zero-shot predictions, while the other two groups of tasks, SuperGLUE [14] and MSGS [15], require finetuning of the submitted models for classification. See Appendix A for the complete list of tasks.
